lines: A separate server process is still a system somebody has to run and keep alive.
What if the engine running your query was just... the process you're already in?
That's where this one goes.
A table already sits in memory, in the exact same process as the engine.
Before SQL can touch it, does that table need to be written out and reloaded first?
Or can the engine just reach into it, right where it already lives?
answer: Nothing gets written out or reloaded first.

lines: Ask for a sum over that in-memory table, and the answer comes back correctly.
Same thing again, a different kind of in-memory table this time.
No conversion step ran in between either time -- the engine just read what was already there.
Values get processed in batches here, not one at a time.
Hand the same question to four workers instead of one, and time how long each takes.
Four comes back well ahead of one -- the batches split cleanly across them.
Now cap how much memory the engine's allowed to use, and ask it to sort more than that.
Does it refuse, or does it find somewhere else to put the overflow?
Watch the disk, not the error log.
answer: The overflow spills to disk, and the sort keeps going.

lines: New files actually appear on disk the moment memory runs out.
The sort still finishes, under the cap the whole time.
Count the rows at the end, and every single one is still there.
A table built by another tool entirely sits on this machine, no server attached to it.
Point this engine straight at it and ask a narrow question.
The plan it produces shows the narrowing happened before most of the file was ever touched.
Swap that table for one built by a completely different storage project.
Same narrow question, same direct connection, no in-between service of any kind.
The right rows come back again, just as directly.
This time the catalog that tracks table versions isn't a separate service at all.
It's rows in an ordinary table, sitting right next to the data.
Write to the table twice, and two separate, queryable versions exist afterward -- recorded as plain rows.
No service to start, no cluster to keep alive, and it still reads every format this chapter built.
Batches processed together, work split across workers, overflow handled without failing.
One sandbox left that can't run any of this directly at all. That one's next.
